Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0, “Detecting Contaminants in Post-Consumer Plastic Packaging Waste by a NIR Hyperspectral Imaging-Based Cascade Detection Approach” (2021), treats plastic-waste management primarily as a sorting-quality problem: post-consumer packaging must be cleaned of impurities before mechanical recycling can be effective. Its main contribution is the use of near-infrared hyperspectral imaging in a cascade-detection framework to identify contaminants inside plastic packaging waste. Paper 1, “Identification of Aged Polypropylene with Machine Learning and Near-Infrared Spectroscopy for Improved Recycling” (2025), builds on the same broad premise—optical sensing can make mixed plastic waste legible—but shifts the target from contaminant detection to material-state recognition. Instead of asking only “Is there an impurity?”, it asks “Can we identify aged polypropylene well enough to improve sorting?” This is an important advance because polymer aging, surface condition, and material history can affect recyclability, meaning that successful recycling depends not only on separating foreign objects but also on distinguishing usable from degraded plastic. The transition therefore moves from impurity screening toward quality-aware plastic classification.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, “Development of an Economically Viable AI-Enabled Sorting Technology for Complex Plastic Waste Streams” (2025), expands the scope again. Where Paper 1 focuses on a specific material class—aged polypropylene—using machine learning and near-infrared spectroscopy, Paper 2 frames the challenge as a system-level sorting problem for complex plastic streams, especially difficult categories such as #3–#7 plastics. Its advance is the integration of artificial intelligence with sensor fusion and an explicit emphasis on economic viability. This matters because real recycling facilities do not only need accurate laboratory-style classification; they need technologies that can operate on heterogeneous, high-throughput waste streams at a cost that facilities can bear. The progression therefore moves from single-purpose contaminant detection, to targeted polymer-condition identification, to a broader AI-enabled sorting architecture designed for industrially complex waste.

Key Turning Points:  
The first turning point is the move from manual or coarse mechanical sorting toward sensor-based characterization. The 2021 paper shows that plastic-waste management can be improved by making contaminants visible through hyperspectral imaging, thereby addressing a core weakness in conventional recycling chains: the inability to systematically identify impurities.  

The second turning point is the recognition that polymer identity alone is insufficient. The 2025 aged-polypropylene paper introduces the idea that material condition—especially aging—must be detected if recycling is to avoid downcycling, mis-sorting, or poor-quality output. This shifts the research emphasis from “what polymer is present?” to “is this polymer still suitable for recycling?”  

The third turning point is the shift from single-sensor analytics to integrated, economically constrained sorting systems. The second 2025 paper treats plastic waste management as an engineering and economic system problem, combining AI with multiple sensing modalities to address hard-to-sort plastics. This marks a conceptual move from analytical detection toward deployable sorting infrastructure.  

Although the graph does not contain explicit predecessor or parallel-work edges, these three papers reveal a clear thematic trajectory: spectroscopy-based detection, machine-learning-based material-state recognition, and AI-enabled sensor-fusion sorting.

Recurring Limitations:  
A recurring limitation across the papers is the difficulty of handling heterogeneous, mixed, contaminated, or aged plastic waste. The 2021 paper emphasizes impurities in post-consumer packaging; the first 2025 paper emphasizes the inefficiency of manual sorting and the challenge of mixed plastics; the second 2025 paper emphasizes the difficulty of sorting complex #3–#7 streams. All three imply that simple, single-step sorting is inadequate for real-world plastic waste.  

Another recurring limitation is the dependence on optical or spectroscopic signals in conditions that are likely to be noisy and variable. Surface contamination, additives, pigments, aging, moisture, multilayer structures, and mixed polymer compositions can all degrade classification performance. The papers advance sensing methods, but they do not fully resolve the scientific problem of robust recognition under uncontrolled, dirty, industrial conditions.  

A third recurring limitation is scalability. - Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0, “Detecting Contaminants in Post-Consumer Plastic Packaging Waste by a NIR Hyperspectral Imaging-Based Cascade Detection Approach” (2021), treats plastic-waste management primarily as a sorting-quality problem: post-consumer packaging must be cleaned of impurities before mechanical recycling can be effective. Its main contribution is the use of near-infrared hyperspectral imaging in a cascade-detection framework to identify contaminants inside plastic packaging waste. Paper 1, “Identification of Aged Polypropylene with Machine Learning and Near-Infrared Spectroscopy for Improved Recycling” (2025), builds on the same broad premise—optical sensing can make mixed plastic waste legible—but shifts the target from contaminant detection to material-state recognition. Instead of asking only “Is there an impurity?”, it asks “Can we identify aged polypropylene well enough to improve sorting?” This is an important advance because polymer aging, surface condition, and material history can affect recyclability, meaning that successful recycling depends not only on separating foreign objects but also on distinguishing usable from degraded plastic. The transition therefore moves from impurity screening toward quality-aware plastic classification.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, “Development of an Economically Viable AI-Enabled Sorting Technology for Complex Plastic Waste Streams” (2025), expands the scope again. Where Paper 1 focuses on a specific material class—aged polypropylene—using machine learning and near-infrared spectroscopy, Paper 2 frames the challenge as a system-level sorting problem for complex plastic streams, especially difficult categories such as #3–#7 plastics. Its advance is the integration of artificial intelligence with sensor fusion and an explicit emphasis on economic viability. This matters because real recycling facilities do not only need accurate laboratory-style classification; they need technologies that can operate on heterogeneous, high-throughput waste streams at a cost that facilities can bear. The progression therefore moves from single-purpose contaminant detection, to targeted polymer-condition identification, to a broader AI-enabled sorting architecture designed for industrially complex waste.

Key Turning Points:  
The first turning point is the move from manual or coarse mechanical sorting toward sensor-based characterization. The 2021 paper shows that plastic-waste management can be improved by making contaminants visible through hyperspectral imaging, thereby addressing a core weakness in conventional recycling chains: the inability to systematically identify impurities.  

The second turning point is the recognition that polymer identity alone is insufficient. The 2025 aged-polypropylene paper introduces the idea that material condition—especially aging—must be detected if recycling is to avoid downcycling, mis-sorting, or poor-quality output. This shifts the research emphasis from “what polymer is present?” to “is this polymer still suitable for recycling?”  

The third turning point is the shift from single-sensor analytics to integrated, economically constrained sorting systems. The second 2025 paper treats plastic waste management as an engineering and economic system problem, combining AI with multiple sensing modalities to address hard-to-sort plastics. This marks a conceptual move from analytical detection toward deployable sorting infrastructure.  

Although the graph does not contain explicit predecessor or parallel-work edges, these three papers reveal a clear thematic trajectory: spectroscopy-based detection, machine-learning-based material-state recognition, and AI-enabled sensor-fusion sorting.

Recurring Limitations:  
A recurring limitation across the papers is the difficulty of handling heterogeneous, mixed, contaminated, or aged plastic waste. The 2021 paper emphasizes impurities in post-consumer packaging; the first 2025 paper emphasizes the inefficiency of manual sorting and the challenge of mixed plastics; the second 2025 paper emphasizes the difficulty of sorting complex #3–#7 streams. All three imply that simple, single-step sorting is inadequate for real-world plastic waste.  

Another recurring limitation is the dependence on optical or spectroscopic signals in conditions that are likely to be noisy and variable. Surface contamination, additives, pigments, aging, moisture, multilayer structures, and mixed polymer compositions can all degrade classification performance. The papers advance sensing methods, but they do not fully resolve the scientific problem of robust recognition under uncontrolled, dirty, industrial conditions.  

A third recurring limitation is scalability. The 2021 paper focuses on detection, the 2025 polypropylene paper on improved identification, and the 2025 sensor-fusion paper on economically viable sorting. However, the broader challenge of translating accurate characterization into reliable, low-cost, high-throughput recycling operations remains only partially solved.

One open scientific problem is robust online characterization of dirty, aged, contaminated, pigmented, multilayer, or additive-laden plastics. Existing NIR-based approaches are promising, but real waste streams contain surface degradation, food residue, labels, inks, fillers, and polymer blends that can obscure or distort spectral signatures. A unresolved challenge is to develop sensing and modeling methods that remain accurate under these conditions without requiring unrealistic sample preparation.  

A second open problem is generalization across waste streams, facilities, instruments, and geographic contexts. Machine-learning models trained on one type of plastic waste may not transfer well to another because composition, contamination levels, aging patterns, and sensor calibration differ. The field still needs scientifically grounded methods for domain adaptation, calibration transfer, uncertainty quantification, and confidence-aware decision-making in sorting systems.  

A third open problem is optimal sensor fusion for plastic waste. Paper 2 points toward sensor fusion, but the scientific question remains: which combinations of spectral, visual, chemical, thermal, density-based, or mechanical signals are most informative for different plastic categories, and how should their outputs be fused under cost, speed, and hardware constraints? This is not merely an engineering issue; it requires understanding which physical properties distinguish recyclable, degraded, contaminated, or hazardous plastics.

These materials are often hard to identify, separate, and recycle because their composition is heterogeneous and their economic value is low. The field has not yet solved how to combine sensing, artificial intelligence, and physical or chemical separation mechanisms in a way that makes these streams reliably recoverable at scale.

ideas.title: Purity-Stream Digital Twin for Plastic Waste: Uncertainty-Aware Spectral Assay and Single-Variety Stream Optimization for Material-Flow Management
ideas.motivation: Better plastic-waste management requires reliable material-flow data, but current sensing studies often stop at item-level polymer or contaminant classification. Mid-infrared machine learning can characterize mixed plastic waste [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252), near-infrared hyperspectral cascade detection can identify contaminants in post-consumer packaging [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), near-infrared machine learning can recognize aged polypropylene [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181), and AI-enabled sensor fusion can target difficult #3-#7 streams [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218). The unresolved bottleneck is not only classification accuracy but conversion of uncertain, dirty, aged, and contaminated sensor observations into auditable material-flow accounts and economically feasible circularity decisions. The proposed method borrows a mechanism from industrial engineering and metal recycling: supply-chain-wide digitalization and single-variety stream optimization under purity and CO2 constraints [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W6905989044). This transfer is non-trivial because plastic streams contain low-value heterogeneous #3-#7 materials, multilayer packaging, pigments, residues, and aged surfaces, so the metal purity-ledger concept must become probabilistic and sensor-driven. The method also adapts false-color flow imaging that links pixel-level spectral classification to bulk mass composition and presentation [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096), and a circularity-pathway decision model for industrial waste streams [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4399957252). The primary testable hypothesis is that organizing uncertain spectral classifications into purity-constrained single-polymer stream ledgers improves material-flow composition accuracy and circularity routing outcomes compared with unstructured aggregation of the same sensor outputs.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the disconnect between online plastic sensing and actionable material-flow management; it can be divided into 4 parts: uncertainty-aware spectral assay, presentation-aware false-color flow assay, purity-constrained single-stream ledger, and circularity routing optimizer.

proposed_method.name: Uncertainty-aware spectral material-state assay
proposed_method.description: Fuse NIR, MIR, hyperspectral, RGB, and optional thermal signals to output calibrated posterior probabilities for polymer type, contaminant presence, aging state, and recyclability. The assay builds on mid-infrared machine learning for mixed plastics [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252), NIR hyperspectral contaminant detection [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), aged-polypropylene identification [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181), and sensor-fusion sorting for difficult #3-#7 plastics [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218).

proposed_method.name: Presentation-aware false-color flow assay
proposed_method.description: Convert pixel- and item-level posteriors into false-color semantic channels for polymer identity, contamination, aging, and recyclability, then train a presentation-aware regression model to estimate bulk mass composition from singulated, monolayer, and bulk flow views. This adapts NIR false-color flow imaging that explicitly couples pixel classification to material-flow composition and presentation [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096).

proposed_method.name: Purity-constrained single-stream ledger
proposed_method.description: Maintain a Bayesian mass balance for each target single-polymer or quality stream, updating expected mass and purity distributions from sensor posteriors and estimated item masses. This adapts single-variety metal-stream optimization and supply-chain-wide digitalization from industrial engineering to plastic waste, replacing deterministic scrap grades with probabilistic purity ledgers [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W6905989044).

proposed_method.name: Circularity routing optimizer
proposed_method.description: Route each purity stream to mechanical recycling, washing, blending, waste-to-fuel, or controlled disposal by maximizing expected economic value and environmental benefit subject to purity chance constraints and capacity limits. The optimizer adapts circularity-pathway decision modeling for industrial waste streams [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4399957252).

ideas.title: Presentation-Aware Stochastic Purity-State Mass-Balance for Uncertainty-Calibrated Plastic Sorting and Material-Flow Accounting
ideas.motivation: Better management of global plastic waste requires reliable, real-time, mass-based data about mixed post-consumer streams, not only item-level labels. Spectroscopy and machine learning can characterize mixed plastics [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252), detect contaminants in packaging waste [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), identify aged polypropylene [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181), and support economically viable AI sorting for complex #3-#7 streams [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218). However, current systems still struggle to convert uncertain, presentation-dependent spectral evidence into stream-level purity, recycling yield, and circular-economy decisions when items are dirty, pigmented, multilayer, or bulk-presented. This idea transfers two cross-domain mechanisms: mixed-pixel spectral unmixing from remote sensing [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3093559484) and uncertain-quality dynamic routing from operations research [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4407267473). It also uses presentation-stratified false-color flow imaging to connect pixel/item evidence to mass flow [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096). The primary testable hypothesis is that a structured stochastic purity-state mass-balance model, explicitly representing occlusion, contaminant carryover, aging degradation, and washing/blending, reduces bulk-composition error and downstream routing loss relative to unstructured posterior aggregation under identical spectral inputs.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve robust material-flow accounting and sorting decisions for dirty, aged, mixed plastic waste; it can be divided into five parts: (1) a presentation-stratified spectral assay, (2) mixed-source spectral unmixing with uncertainty, (3) a stochastic purity-state mass-balance model, (4) an identifiability and error-bound analysis for presentation-dependent bulk composition, and (5) decision-aware calibration and chance-constrained routing.

proposed_method.name: Presentation-stratified false-color flow assay
proposed_method.description: Create or augment NIR/MIR measurements in singulated, monolayer, and bulk presentations, using false-color channels that summarize informative spectral bands [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096). Record known mass fractions of polymer categories, contaminants, labels, inks, moisture, pigments, and aged states, building on contaminant detection [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653) and aged-polymer identification [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181). MIR can provide complementary polymer chemistry where needed [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252). Presentation is an explicit variable because occlusion and packing alter observed spectra and mass-flow aggregation [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096).

proposed_method.name: Mixed-source spectral unmixing with uncertainty
proposed_method.description: Model each pixel, item, or bulk spectrum as a mixture of endmembers rather than a single resin label, borrowing mixed-pixel unmixing and weathering/contamination-aware feature selection from remote sensing [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3093559484). Endmembers include polymer type, aged polymer state, food residue, labels, inks, additives, pigments, moisture, and multilayer contributions. The model outputs posterior abundance distributions and confidence estimates, extending online spectroscopy-based plastic characterization [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252) and contaminant/aging detection [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181). Low-confidence observations are flagged for conservative routing [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3093559484).

proposed_method.name: Stochastic purity-state mass-balance model
proposed_method.description: Represent each stream as a mass vector over polymer classes, aging grades, contaminants, additives, moisture, and non-plastic impurities. Define stochastic transition kernels for sorting, washing, shredding, density separation, blending, and extrusion that encode contaminant carryover, aging degradation, removal efficiency, and dilution. Add a presentation-dependent observation model linking true mass state to false-color sensor channels under singulated, monolayer, and bulk flow, including occlusion and item-mass uncertainty. This adapts the operations-research mechanism of uncertain material quality as a dynamic decision state [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4407267473) to sensor-based recycling lines, and it differs from simple classifier aggregation by predicting how purity evolves across unit operations. The resulting state estimates support facility-level material-flow accounting and complex-stream sorting decisions [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218).

proposed_method.name: Presentation identifiability and error-bound analysis
proposed_method.description: Derive bounds on bulk mass-composition error from false-color semantic channels as functions of presentation, occlusion probability, item-mass variance, endmember collinearity, and sensor noise. This analysis specifies when bulk composition is identifiable from singulated, monolayer, or bulk observations and distinguishes the assay from ordinary pixel-classification aggregation [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4324031096). The bounds are used to set conservative uncertainty thresholds and to choose presentation-specific routing policies, following uncertainty-aware detection logic from remote sensing [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3093559484).

proposed_method.name: Decision-aware calibration and chance-constrained routing
proposed_method.description: Calibrate the unmixing posteriors and sorting thresholds using downstream economic and environmental loss rather than classification accuracy alone. The routing optimizer chooses recycling, downcycling, rejection, or waste-to-fuel diversion under chance constraints on purity and yield, adapting dynamic multi-period recycling routing under uncertain material quality [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4407267473). This closed-loop decision layer is intended to keep sorting actions economically viable for hard-to-recycle #3-#7 streams [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218) and to produce uncertainty-aware material-flow data for interventions such as bottle recycling, bag reduction, or fuel substitution.

Keep this model fixed for the primary hypothesis test. Derive presentation identifiability bounds before evaluating flow-accounting models.

Keep the instrument fixed and repeat scans of unchanged streams to rule out drift. Run diagnostic component-alone controls after the primary test: unmixing-only, presentation-only regression, and process-only with oracle labels.

Mechanism isolation: After a structured-model advantage is established, disable one mechanism at a time: occlusion observation, contaminant carryover, aging degradation, and washing/blending transitions. Compare each disabled model with the full model under singulated, monolayer, and bulk presentations to attribute gains to the claimed mechanisms rather than generic smoothing.

Decision calibration phase: With the best mass-balance model fixed, compare standard temperature or cross-entropy calibration against decision-aware calibration that minimizes routing loss [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4407267473). Vary only the calibration objective. Metrics are contamination risk, recyclate yield, chance-constraint violation, and expected economic/environmental objective for recycling, downcycling, or waste-to-fuel routing.

Scope and generalization: Test the validated pipeline on unseen waste streams, facilities, or instruments, focusing on difficult #3-#7 plastics and economically constrained sorting [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218). Evaluate whether presentation-stratified stochastic mass-balance maintains lower composition error and routing loss than baselines under domain shift.

ideas.motivation: Better plastic-waste management requires reliable stream-level data and sorting decisions that remain valid for dirty, aged, contaminated, pigmented, multilayer, and #3-#7 plastics. Spectroscopic machine learning can characterize mixed plastic waste [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252), NIR hyperspectral cascade detection can identify contaminants in post-consumer packaging [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), NIR machine learning can recognize aged polypropylene [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181), and AI-enabled sensor-fusion sorting targets economically viable handling of complex streams [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218). However, these approaches still mostly infer local labels or categories, while industrial streams contain overlapping, occluded, and presentation-dependent observations that must be converted into mass-balanced flow data for circular-economy decisions. Integrated material flow analysis provides the accounting structure needed to support material efficiency [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4286698685), remote sensing provides spectral unmixing and uncertainty-aware inversion for mixed scenes [Author et al., 2012](https://openalex.org/W2265885259), and hierarchical deep sorting shows how pairwise discrimination can be organized into circular plastic upgrading [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2988016874). The unresolved bottleneck is not another classifier but a controlled inference system that treats physical presentation as an active variable, conserves mass across unit operations, and quantifies identifiability limits.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve robust stream-level characterization and material-flow accounting for mixed, occluded, contaminated, aged plastics; it can be divided into 4 parts: (1) a presentation-conditioned spectral unmixing observation model, (2) a differentiable mass-balance filter with conservation constraints and unit-operation transition kernels, (3) an identifiability-driven active presentation controller, and (4) a material-flow translation layer for recycling-yield and circular-economy decisions. The primary testable hypothesis is that uncertainty-directed active presentation reduces bulk-composition estimation error and sorting misallocation relative to fixed or random presentation under equal sensing, actuation, and throughput budgets.

proposed_method.name: Presentation-conditioned spectral unmixing
proposed_method.description: The observation model treats each conveyor view as a mixed scene rather than a clean isolated item, adapting remote-sensing unmixing and uncertainty-aware retrieval to plastic waste [Author et al., 2012](https://openalex.org/W2265885259). It ingests NIR, MIR, RGB, or false-color band ratios and explicitly conditions the likelihood on presentation variables such as singulation, overlap, layer thickness, belt speed, orientation, and view geometry. This extends prior spectroscopic plastic characterization [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4309475252), contaminant detection [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3176826653), aged-polymer recognition [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4408188181), and sensor-fusion sorting [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218) by outputting posterior probabilities and calibrated uncertainties for polymer grade, contamination, aging, and recyclability states instead of only hard labels.

proposed_method.name: Differentiable mass-balance filter
proposed_method.description: A differentiable filter maintains nonnegative mass states for polymer grade, contamination level, aging state, and process stream, using integrated material-flow accounting as the physical backbone [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4286698685). The state transition equation couples unit operations such as singulation, washing, shredding, blending, rejection, and fuel diversion through learned but constrained transition kernels. Because the observation model is presentation-dependent, the filter jointly learns observation biases and transition kernels while enforcing mass conservation, nonnegativity, and known item-mass distributions. This separation allows the system to distinguish measurement error from true contaminant carryover or aging degradation.

proposed_method.name: Identifiability-driven active presentation controller
proposed_method.description: The controller makes presentation an actively controlled inference variable rather than a passive stratification label. It derives identifiability conditions and error bounds for recovering bulk mass composition from occluded bulk presentations using item-mass distributions, false-color channels, and presentation actions. At run time it selects the action that maximizes expected reduction in posterior mass-balance uncertainty per unit cost, such as slowing the belt, increasing singulation, reducing layer thickness, flipping or rescanning uncertain items, or diverting a small sample for higher-cost MIR analysis. The hierarchical escalation follows the deep-sorting logic of pairwise discrimination and selective re-inspection [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2988016874), while the uncertainty-based inversion follows remote-sensing retrieval practice [Author et al., 2012](https://openalex.org/W2265885259). Economic and throughput constraints are included as explicit costs, reflecting the need for viable industrial sorting [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7128697218).

proposed_method.name: Material-flow translation and decision support
proposed_method.description: The posterior mass states are aggregated into material-flow accounts for input, recovered recyclate, reject, downcycled material, and waste-to-fuel streams. This layer converts item-level state probabilities into mass-balanced estimates of recycling yield, contamination risk, and circular-economy performance, following integrated MFA principles [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4286698685). It can support operational routing and policy-relevant scenarios such as bottle recovery, bag reduction, and plastics-to-fuel diversion, while preserving uncertainty rather than collapsing the stream into brittle point estimates.

Secondary scope after core validation: Test real dirty post-consumer streams, different instruments, facilities, and geographic waste compositions. Evaluate domain adaptation and calibration transfer while keeping the primary architecture fixed, and report whether active presentation still reduces error under domain shift.

Decision impact: Use the posterior mass-flow estimates to simulate or operate routing decisions for recycling, rejection, downcycling, and fuel diversion.
